sections.title: Pain points apparel brands and retailers face without RFID
bullets: Retailer mandate deadlines — Walmart, Target, and Macy's require item-level RFID tagging; suppliers failing compliance face chargebacks of $25-$50 per non-compliant case and risk losing shelf placement entirely.

Inventory accuracy stuck at 65-75% — manual barcode cycle counts take 3-5 days per store, leaving floor staff unable to locate sizes and colors, causing lost sales estimated at 4-8% of annual revenue.

Checkout shrink and shoplifting — apparel retailers lose 1.4-1.8% of revenue to shrink annually; standard EAS tags provide no inventory data and require separate RFID infrastructure to be added later.

BOPIS and ship-from-store failures — without real-time item-level visibility, 12-18% of online orders placed against store inventory are cancelled at fulfillment because the item cannot be located in time.
Source tagging logistics — applying tags at the distribution center rather than the factory adds $0.08-$0.15 per unit in labor, versus $0.02-$0.04 when applied at the source during garment finishing.

sections.title: Retailer mandate landscape — Walmart, Target, Macy's, Nordstrom, Nike, Inditex, H&M, Kohl's and their encoding specifics
sections.intro: The apparel RFID landscape in 2026 is mandate-driven. Tier-1 retailers have converged on a tightly specified item-level tagging regime that suppliers must satisfy down to the GS1 Company Prefix, SGTIN-96 partition value, filter value, chip performance class and Auburn ARC-certified inlay size. A supplier whose tags miss any of these specs faces chargebacks, vendor-scorecard degradation and — in repeated cases — shelf-space reallocation. The detailed mandate map below is the playbook our compliance team uses with every new apparel programme.
bullets: Walmart RFID Tier-1 mandate — began 2020 with apparel and accessories, expanded 2022 to home and entertainment, 2024-2025 phase adding hardlines (toys, sporting goods, electronics). SGTIN-96 encoding with partition derived from the supplier's GS1 Company Prefix (typically partition value 5 or 6 for 7-8 digit prefixes), filter value 1 for item-level tags. Tags must pass Auburn RFID Lab ARC certification at the inlay size and chip class specified for the category (ARC Spec L1/L2/L3 for apparel, M7 for footwear and hard-goods). Chargebacks start at USD 25 per case on missing tags and USD 3 per unit on encoding errors; repeat non-compliance triggers quarterly supplier-scorecard review and risk of delisting. Compliance pack: 100% read rate at Walmart receiving-dock portal, 99%+ encoding accuracy per pre-ship audit, EPC URI format in the ASN EDI 856 transmission.

Target item-level RFID programme — in-force across apparel, accessories and beauty since 2022, expanded to home goods 2024. SGTIN-96 with Target-specified filter value 1 for retail-item tier. Required inlay sizes reference Auburn ARC Spec B (~70×14mm for hangtag) or Spec L (~44×44mm for care-label variant). Tags must be Impinj M730/M750/M800 class or NXP UCODE 9 class (older UCODE 8 accepted only with extended read-zone validation). Target's receiving portal at regional DCs runs multi-antenna Zebra FX9600 arrays; missed-read rates above 2% trigger supplier remediation. Target also requires EPCIS 1.2 object-event capture at the finished-goods DC for their supply-chain visibility programme.

Macy's and Nordstrom — Macy's mandate began 2013 (among the earliest majors) and covers apparel, intimate apparel, accessories and beauty with SGTIN-96 + filter value 1 encoding; Macy's accepts a wider range of Auburn ARC classes but specifies a 97%+ first-pass read at receiving. Nordstrom mandate added apparel, accessories and beauty 2022-2024 with SGTIN-96 encoding and Nordstrom-provided 'RFID Technical Playbook' updated annually; Nordstrom operates a supplier-compliance portal where pre-ship encoding validation CSV files are uploaded before shipment release.

Inditex / Zara leadership posture — Inditex ran one of the earliest at-scale retail RFID programmes from 2007, first on UCODE G2iM, migrating to UCODE 7 by 2014, UCODE 8 by 2019, and UCODE 9 by 2022. Zara stores internally achieve 97-99% inventory accuracy versus the 65-75% cycle-count industry baseline. Inditex publishes SGTIN-96 encoding specifications to its thousands of apparel suppliers globally, with most suppliers using Avery Dennison Smartrac AD-226u7 or equivalent Impinj M730-based inlays. The programme is a de-facto reference benchmark for apparel RFID operations worldwide.

Nike, H&M Group and Kohl's — Nike RFID programme covers all global footwear (over 1 billion units annually) with UCODE 9-class performance inlays in the shoe-box source-tag position; Nike-specified encoding uses custom 128-bit identifier with GS1 prefix compatibility. H&M Group rolled out item-level RFID across all banners (H&M, H&M Home, Cos, & Other Stories, Arket, Weekday, Monki) 2022-2024 with SGTIN-96 + Impinj Monza R6 or M730 class silicon. Kohl's mandate (2021 onward) covers apparel, accessories and footwear with SGTIN-96 + Auburn ARC Spec B/L inlay certification.

EU retail posture — Decathlon has run item-level RFID in stores since 2014 with UCODE 8 and UCODE 9 chips, achieving 98% inventory accuracy across 1,700+ stores globally; Decathlon's programme is referenced by the European RFID Research Centre as a benchmark under the CEN CWA 16924 EU retail privacy framework. Tesco, Marks & Spencer, Uniqlo, C&A and Primark all operate item-level RFID at varying maturity, most specifying Gen2 v2 Untraceable command support (CEN CWA 16924 mandates this for post-sale consumer privacy).

Auburn University RFID Lab ARC Program — the de facto US retail-industry certification lab for inlay performance testing. ARC issues inlay-spec certifications (Spec A through Spec M, plus footwear Spec M7 and logistics Spec U) rating the inlay across test scenarios: near-metal, through-liquid, through-cardboard, orientation robustness, and read-zone coverage patterns. Retailer mandates reference specific ARC specs as the minimum admissible inlay. Spec L (44×44mm for care-label) and Spec B (70×14mm for hangtag) are the two most-cited in apparel mandates. ARC certification is typically USD 3,000-8,000 per inlay design with 4-6 week turnaround at Auburn, refreshed annually as new chip generations launch.

Chargeback economics and ROI of compliance — a 100,000-unit apparel shipment to Walmart with a 2% encoding-error rate triggers USD 6,000 in per-unit chargebacks (2% × 100k × USD 3) plus USD 2,500 in case-level chargebacks if 2% of cases are missing tags entirely (say 500 cases × USD 5); total USD 8,500 on a single shipment. Over a year of weekly shipments, non-compliance chargebacks can run USD 400-800k per supplier-retailer relationship. Full mandate compliance via Proud Tek factory-encoded source tags typically costs USD 0.06-0.10 per unit all-in (tag + encoding + QA), vs USD 0.20-0.35 per unit if tagging is added at the US DC — a 3-4× programme-level cost advantage alongside the chargeback avoidance.

sections.title: Factory source-tagging operations — cut-and-sew tier integration, garment finishing and converter workflow
sections.intro: Apparel RFID's real economic leverage is at the point of garment finishing, not at the DC. Factory source-tagging — where the RFID tag is applied during the garment's manufacturing sequence rather than retrofitted downstream — is the line between a compliance programme that costs USD 0.06/unit and one that costs USD 0.25/unit. The operational detail of how a source-tagging line is integrated into cut-and-sew facilities in Vietnam, Bangladesh, China, India, Cambodia and Turkey is the implementation knowledge that separates turnkey programmes from chronic-remediation programmes.
bullets: Attachment method and where in the sewing sequence the tag enters — woven care labels with an embedded RFID inlay are sewn into the neck seam or side seam alongside the regular content/care label during the normal finishing operation (typically the last 30 seconds of the garment-sewing sequence, after the neck-binder operation and before final press); UHF hang tags are attached at the kimble-gun station in finishing, typically adjacent to the final-QC station before folding and bagging; heat-transfer labels integrate at the same station with a 20-second thermoheader press cycle; sewn-in waistband / care-label variants integrate at mid-sewing before the side-seam closure. Proud Tek ships each of these four attachment-method SKUs with factory-applied encoding and serialized CSV mapping file.

Converter and inlay-to-label conversion workflow — raw UHF inlay (e.g., Avery AD-226u7, Smartrac DogBone U9, Arizon AZ-9629) arrives at the label converter on 100m or 300m reels, is laminated to a printable PET or Tyvek facestock at the converter (Avery Dennison Monarch, CCL Label, LabelTape, Brady GraphTex or similar), pre-printed with the retailer's required barcode and artwork, die-cut to the Auburn ARC-specified dimension, encoded with the EPC serial via an SATO CX4DT, Zebra ZT411 RFID or Toshiba B-EX4T1 RFID printer-encoder, and shipped on reels to the garment factory. Converter tier capacity in Asia is dominated by Avery Dennison (Hong Kong + Shanghai + Shenzhen + Guangzhou), R-Pac (Shanghai + Vietnam), CCL Industries, and regional converters like Shangdong Smartrac, Shenzhen Shengli Label and several Vietnam-based converters serving Nike / Adidas / VF Corp.

Encoding equipment on the garment-factory floor — factory-side encoding (rather than converter-side) is used when per-garment serialization must reference a garment-ID barcode scanned at the final-inspection station. Typical setup: SATO CL4NX-J RFID or Zebra ZT411 with RFID encoder module, drop-in UHF reader (Impinj R420 or Zebra FX7500) at the scanning station, WMS / ERP integration via REST webhook to assign a per-garment serial from a Company-Prefix-scoped serial pool. Tag encoding verification is performed in-line with a <100ms per-tag cycle; failed encodings are rejected via air-jet diverter into a scrap bin. Production throughput reaches 2,000-4,000 garments/hour per line.

BOM economics and cost allocation — fully-loaded cost of factory-applied RFID source tag breakdown: UHF inlay USD 0.025-0.045 at 1M+ volume (strap assembly + reference antenna converter cost); facestock, print and die-cut USD 0.008-0.015 per label; encoding operation USD 0.002-0.005 per tag (throughput-amortized equipment cost + operator labor); application labor at garment-factory USD 0.005-0.012 per garment (a few seconds of operator motion to tag-and-kimble); total USD 0.04-0.08 per garment at converter-encoded scale. Compared to DC tagging at USD 0.20-0.35 per unit (higher tag cost in small-volume buys + US-hourly labor to retrofit), source tagging saves USD 0.14-0.28 per unit or USD 14-28 per 100 units shipped.

Tier-1 apparel factory RFID-readiness audit — key dimensions to validate before going to volume: does the factory already have RFID printer-encoders at the finishing station, or do we ship pre-encoded tags? does the factory's MES/ERP system support per-garment serial-number assignment? is there a dedicated QA station for RFID encoded-tag verification (reading 100% of encoded tags before cartonization)? is cartonization-level scanning in place to generate ASN EDI 856 transmissions with EPC URIs? is the factory ISO 9001 certified and does it participate in the retailer-specific compliance audit programme (Walmart GRS, Target FSI)? Proud Tek ships tags to 2,000+ apparel factories globally; we maintain a factory-readiness registry to route pre-encoded vs factory-encoded SKU specifications based on each factory's infrastructure tier.

Nike / Adidas / VF Corp source-tag posture — large athletic-brand programmes operate with tag converter relationships that often predate the retailer-mandate era. Nike Direct works with R-Pac and Avery Dennison for footwear and apparel source tagging in Vietnam, Cambodia and Indonesia; Adidas operates with Avery Dennison Brazil and Smartrac Germany for Adidas North America and EU programmes respectively; VF Corporation (The North Face, Vans, Timberland, Dickies) runs a central Avery Dennison programme with factory-applied source tagging at 90%+ SKU coverage. Proud Tek's programme frequently serves second-source and regional-override cases where the tier-1 converter cannot meet lead-time or regional-preference requirements.

Retailer-specific quality audits and TID inspection — most major mandate retailers perform inbound encoding audits at the regional DC: 100 tags from each shipment are read with a Zebra MC3300 handheld, EPC decoded and compared to the ASN-declared payload, TID field cross-checked against the inlay chip class specified in the mandate (e.g., UCODE 9 TID prefix 0xE2801170 / model ID 0x110 required for Walmart Tier-1 apparel). Factories using counterfeit 'UCODE 9 compatible' silicon (often UCODE 7 re-marked with falsified TID) get detected on TID audit and face rejection of the entire shipment plus supplier-compliance escalation. Proud Tek maintains chip-authenticity clauses in every factory supply agreement to prevent this failure class.

Sample-run-to-mass-production progression — standard apparel source-tagging programme lifecycle: 500-unit sample run for retailer-mandate verification (6-8 weeks from PO including Auburn ARC validation if the inlay is new); pilot production of 10,000-50,000 units across 2-5 SKUs (4-6 weeks); first mass-production shipment 50,000-500,000 units (2-4 weeks per wave); steady-state weekly shipments thereafter at the brand's normal garment-production cadence. Proud Tek's typical apparel-brand relationship reaches steady state in 14-18 weeks from initial RFI.

sections.title: In-store deployment — Zebra / Impinj reader infrastructure, handhelds, fitting rooms and converged EAS
sections.intro: Item-level RFID's store-floor impact depends as much on the reader network as on the tag. A well-executed in-store deployment combines fixed receiving-dock portals, overhead storage-room inventory readers, handheld cycle-counting devices, fitting-room proximity readers and EAS-converged exit readers — each with specific RF design, antenna placement and software integration requirements. The paragraphs below reflect how Tier-1 specialty apparel and department-store deployments are operationally scoped.
bullets: Receiving-dock portal reader setup — 4-port Impinj R700 or R420, or Zebra FX9600, with 2-4 Times-7 A5010 or MTI MT-261021 RHCP antennas arranged in a goalposts pattern at the dock-door opening. Operating at 30 dBm ERP (FCC) or 2 W ERP (ETSI), typical read rate for a pallet of 600 apparel items in retail-ready packaging is 99%+ first-pass within 20 seconds of pallet movement. ASN EDI 856 reconciliation runs via middleware (Impinj ItemSense, Zebra Savanna, PervasiveTags, CSL ReaderConfigurator) with automatic rejection flagging for missing-tag cases and encoding anomalies. Dock-door read accuracy is the single most-audited store-RFID KPI for retailer-mandate compliance.

Back-of-house inventory reader network — 8-32 fixed Impinj xArray or Zebra ATR7000 overhead readers mounted in stockroom ceiling grids, reading tagged inventory every 5-15 minutes for continuous replenishment visibility. Typical specialty-apparel store (2,500-5,000 sqft sales floor + 1,000-2,000 sqft stockroom) uses 4-8 xArray units; flagship department stores (50,000+ sqft) deploy 40-120 units. Software integration via Impinj ItemSense publishes item location (zone-level resolution ~5m) to the retailer's inventory system in real time, enabling ship-from-store and store-pick-up fulfillment paths that require item-level location data.

Handheld cycle-counting devices — Zebra MC3300xR with RFID module or dedicated Zebra RFD40 Bluetooth sled (attached to TC21/TC26 scanner), Impinj Speedway Xspan handheld, CSL CS108 or Alien ALH-9010. Used for weekly or daily full-store cycle counts (completing a 5,000-SKU store in 20-45 minutes, vs 3-5 days for barcode cycle counting). Count accuracy typically 97-99% on properly tagged inventory; staff training cadence 1-2 hours initial + 30-minute quarterly refresh, usually folded into existing operations training programmes. The transition from full-store barcode cycle counts to 15-minute RFID sweeps is the single largest operational savings in apparel RFID ROI models.

Fitting-room and proximity reader placements — Impinj xSpan or xArray at ceiling-mounted positions above fitting-room clusters, providing zone-level awareness of which items entered fitting rooms (useful for tracking try-on conversion, shrinkage prevention, and identifying trending sizes / colors for replenishment). EAS-converged fitting-room readers alert on exits of items still carrying RFID tags (potential lift prevention), integrated with Checkpoint or Sensormatic EAS pedestal systems at the store exit. The combined hard-tag + RFID deployment (EAS-tuned hard tag with UHF inlay) eliminates the parallel-system redundancy of 2010s-era deployments.

Mobile POS and self-checkout integration — RFID-enabled iPad-based mobile POS (Zebra TC21-RFID, Infinite Peripherals Infinea Tab M, CSL RAIN-based sleds) allows store associates to complete sale transactions from the floor, automatically populating the transaction with scanned RFID items. Self-checkout kiosks with RFID tunnel readers (e.g., Sensormatic Synergy, Datalogic EZ-RFID) read all items in a customer's basket in a single scan cycle, accelerating throughput at unstaffed lanes; Uniqlo's global self-checkout rollout (2018-2024) is the most-cited case study, processing 50-80% of transactions through RFID tunnels with 3-5x checkout-time reduction vs barcode-scan lanes.

POS-bridge and inventory decrement workflow — SGTIN-decoded at POS is translated to the retailer's SKU via GTIN lookup, inventory is decremented in real-time in the central inventory system (typically SAP S/4HANA Retail, Oracle Retail Merchandising, or Manhattan Associates WMS), and the EPCIS event is captured for post-transaction anti-fraud and returns processing. Returns flow is the underappreciated benefit: an RFID-tagged return can be validated as genuine by reading the SGTIN at the return counter, cross-referenced against the original transaction EPCIS event; reduces return fraud (which averages 8-12% of return transaction count in apparel) by 40-60% in mature deployments.

Reader-installation and certification logistics — store-side reader installation typically runs USD 5-15k per store in hardware (4-6 readers at USD 600-1,500 each + antennas + cabling + mounting) plus USD 3-8k in site-survey, installation labor and software integration. Networking requirements modest (PoE+ switches with 2-4 dedicated ports per store, 100 Mbps uplink minimum); RF-survey phase uses Wi-Fi-Explorer or Ekahau RFID modules to validate antenna placements pre-installation. Large-chain rollouts (500-2,000+ stores) typically sequence 10-30 stores per week with a dedicated installation-contractor team; end-to-end rollout timelines run 6-24 months for national chains.

Commercial reader software platforms — Impinj ItemSense (subscription USD 3-8 per store per month), Zebra MotionWorks Enterprise, PervasiveTags, Manhattan RFID, Infor Nexus RFID, Tecsys Elite RFID, and custom-built platforms at Walmart / Target / Nordstrom. Platform selection usually follows the retailer's existing WMS / ERP stack — a Manhattan WMS shop goes to Manhattan RFID, an SAP shop typically integrates Infor or a custom Impinj-native platform. Proud Tek's tag shipments are fully compatible with every major platform because the SGTIN-96 encoding is platform-agnostic at the air-interface layer.

Multi-tag interference and dense-environment tuning — apparel stores with 10,000-50,000 tagged items and 20-60 active readers require careful RF planning to avoid reader-to-reader interference (regulated via TDMA scheduling in modern reader firmware), backscatter collision (mitigated by Gen2 v2 Session 1/2/3/4 session selection), and tag-orientation variance (addressed by dual-polarization antenna deployments). Dense-reader-mode operation at Miller 8 encoding, 160kHz BLF, with session 2 selection is the typical store-configuration baseline; Tier-1 retailers maintain validated reader-firmware-and-configuration bundles distributed through software update cycles.

sections.title: Omnichannel ROI and measured case studies — inventory accuracy, BOPIS, markdown, shrink and returns
sections.intro: The business case for apparel RFID has moved well past the early compliance-driven phase. Retailers with 3+ years of at-scale RFID operations consistently report quantified lifts across five KPI families: inventory accuracy, BOPIS / ship-from-store fulfillment, markdown optimization, shrink reduction and return-fraud reduction. The case studies below aggregate publicly-reported numbers from Inditex, Zara, Decathlon, H&M, Nike, Uniqlo, Lululemon and Macy's alongside Proud Tek programme data, and map directly to the line items that drive the typical 12-18 month payback for a tier-1 apparel retailer.
bullets: Inventory accuracy uplift is the foundational KPI — every other benefit depends on it. Industry-reference barcode-cycle-count baselines sit at 65-75% inventory accuracy (meaning the system-recorded stock position diverges from physical stock by 25-35% of SKUs at any point in time). Mature item-level RFID deployments at Inditex, Decathlon and Lululemon report sustained 97-99% accuracy. At the SKU level this matters most for fast-turning basics (accuracy degrades fastest on high-velocity SKUs) and for seasonal / trend apparel where a single missing size-colour can cost a sale that cannot be recovered. Auburn University's RFID Lab has measured a 13-point average accuracy lift across 18+ published retailer case studies, with the lift holding steady at 96%+ when weekly RFID cycle counts are operationalised.

BOPIS and ship-from-store fulfillment rates — without item-level accuracy, online-order-against-store-inventory cancellation rates run 12-18% (order placed, store cannot locate the unit in time, cancellation issued). After RFID rollout with 97%+ accuracy, cancellation rates drop to 3-6% — a 60-75% reduction in unfulfilled orders. For a USD 500M omnichannel retailer with 30% of online orders fulfilled from store inventory, a 10-point cancellation-rate improvement is USD 15M of recovered gross merchandise value annually. Lululemon's 2022-2024 ship-from-store programme cites RFID-enabled inventory accuracy as the enabler for their same-day delivery rollout.

Markdown optimization and inventory turnover — accurate real-time sell-through data lets merchandising teams trigger markdowns earlier on slow-moving colour-sizes before competitors discount the category. H&M Group's 2023 investor-day disclosure cited RFID-enabled markdown timing as contributing to a 180-basis-point gross-margin improvement over the 2021-2023 period. Inditex's Zara banner famously rebalances inventory across its 2,200+ stores twice per week using RFID accuracy data; the resulting markdown rate (percentage of units sold at full price) is 85%+ versus industry average of 50-60%, a gap driven substantially by the ability to transfer inventory to where it will sell at full price.

Shrink and loss-prevention economics — apparel-retail shrink averages 1.4-1.8% of revenue (including shoplifting, internal theft, process errors and administrative loss). Converged EAS+RFID hard-tag deployments have documented shrink reductions of 40-55% at pilot stores (bringing shrink from ~1.7% to ~0.9% of revenue). Revenue lift of 0.6-0.8 percentage points on a USD 500M retailer is USD 3-4M annually, typically at 80%+ incremental margin since the goods were already in inventory. The Macy's / Nordstrom class of deployments reports an additional ~15% reduction in process-error shrink (transfers, receiving errors, count errors) attributable to the higher inventory accuracy baseline.

Return-fraud reduction — apparel returns average 15-25% of online orders and 8-15% of in-store transactions, with an estimated 8-12% of returns involving some form of fraud (wardrobing, receipt-fraud, stolen-goods returns, used-for-an-event returns). RFID-based return validation — reading the SGTIN at the return counter, cross-referencing the EPCIS event against the original transaction — has measured return-fraud reduction of 40-60% at retailers with 2+ years of deployment maturity. For a USD 500M retailer with a 20% return rate and 10% fraud rate on returns, a 50% fraud-reduction is USD 5M of recovered revenue annually.

Nike RFID and footwear programme economics — Nike's global footwear RFID programme (1B+ units/year) cites three primary business drivers: counterfeit detection at retailer inspection points (TID-based chip-authenticity checks), supply-chain visibility from factory-to-DC-to-store, and in-store inventory accuracy at Nike-owned retail including Nike flagship stores. Nike's 2023 ESG report disclosed that RFID-enabled supply-chain transparency was a key enabler for their Scope 3 emissions reporting programme, showing how RFID ROI extends beyond merchandising into ESG and compliance lines.

Uniqlo and self-checkout case study — Fast Retailing / Uniqlo rolled out RFID self-checkout across 2,200+ stores globally between 2018 and 2024, processing 50-80% of transactions through RFID-tunnel checkout kiosks. Business-case disclosures cite 30-40% reduction in checkout labor hours, 3-5× checkout-time reduction per transaction, improved customer-satisfaction scores on queue-time metrics, and secondary benefits from the RFID tags enabling per-item inventory accuracy (Uniqlo reports 98%+ inventory accuracy globally). The Uniqlo case is the most-cited operational proof point for RFID self-checkout at consumer-fashion scale.

Programme-level ROI and payback — a typical Tier-1 apparel retailer with USD 300M-1B revenue implementing full item-level RFID (source tagging + in-store readers + software + operations) invests USD 5-15M over 18-24 months for tag infrastructure (tags at USD 0.06-0.10/unit × 20-100M annual units) and USD 2-8M for in-store reader and software deployment. Annual benefit realization at maturity is typically USD 12-40M across the five KPI families above, giving a 12-18 month programme-level payback. Proud Tek's apparel-programme customers track against this ROI model from month 3 of rollout, with first BOPIS / inventory-accuracy benefits arriving as early as month 6 after source-tagging starts hitting stores.

Quantified Proud Tek customer outcomes — one 600-door Walmart apparel supplier achieved 100% mandate compliance 8 weeks early and avoided USD 180,000 in forecasted chargebacks; a mid-size specialty retailer improved accuracy from 71% to 97% in 60 days and recovered USD 2.1M in BOPIS revenue; a 40-store mall retailer reduced shrink from 1.7% to 0.9% and saved USD 850,000 in year one; a 12M-unit-per-year apparel brand saved USD 1.4M by moving from DC tagging to Proud Tek factory-encoded source tagging. These are the quantified outcomes we underwrite every new apparel-programme engagement against.
